summary: A framework document that describes and motivates Source Address Validation Improvement (SAVI) methods, which stop nodes on the same IP link from spoofing each other's addresses. It complements ingress filtering with finer-grained checks; specific methods are defined elsewhere.

plainLanguage.summary: In a classroom, nobody should pretend to be another kid when passing notes. SAVI checks the sender's name on every note.

questions: how to prevent ip source address spoofing on a link
how does source address validation improvement work
what is a savi protection perimeter
subtitle: The framework behind SAVI: checking, per host, that packets on a link carry the source address that host is allowed to use.

tldr.problem: The Internet architecture does not prevent IP source address spoofing, and ingress filtering only checks at the granularity of whole networks, so hosts on one link can still impersonate each other.
tldr.mechanism: A SAVI instance watches address assignment packets, binds each legitimate address to a link-layer binding anchor, and drops packets whose source address does not match the anchor.
tldr.outcome: It complements ingress filtering with validation of individual addresses. It is a framework: specific methods are defined in other documents.

today: RFC 7039 is an Informational framework from October 2013, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the design, while specific methods are defined in other documents.

sections.title: Why Source Addresses Need Validating
sections.content:
Hosts use a packet's IP source address to learn where it came from and where to send replies. Because the source address plays no role in forwarding, a sending host can pick it arbitrarily without hurting delivery. Spoofing can therefore enable impersonation, concealment and malicious traffic redirection.

Ingress filtering ([BCP38], [BCP84]) is the widely deployed standard fix, but it works at the granularity of networks: it checks that the prefix of a source address routes to the network the packet came from. Finer-grained validation would keep source address information accurate, reduce the ability to launch denial-of-service attacks, and help find misbehaving hosts.

The Source Address Validation Improvement (SAVI) method complements ingress filtering at the granularity of individual IP addresses. It prevents hosts attached to the same link from spoofing each other's addresses. It was designed to be modular and extensible, and this document describes and motivates that design. It also notes the privacy considerations in RFC 6959.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can write any return address on a letter. SAVI checks that each kid on the street only uses their own house number.

sections.title: The Three-Step Model
sections.content:
SAVI is purely network based, so it needs no support from hosts. A SAVI instance enforces legitimate source addresses in three steps.

  1. Identify which source addresses are legitimate for a host by monitoring packets the host exchanges.
  2. Bind a legitimate address to a binding anchor, a link-layer property of the host's network attachment. It must be verifiable in every packet the host sends and harder to spoof than the IP address itself.
  3. Enforce that source addresses in packets match the anchors they were bound to.

An instance can sit in the hosts' default router, which leaves local traffic unchecked, or in a switch between the hosts and the router, which can check local traffic too. The closer an instance is to the host, the more effective it is, because identification, anchor selection and enforcement are all easier and more reliable near the host. The preferred location is in switches that attach directly to the hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: Watch who gets which house number, remember the kid's front door, and then check every letter against the door it came from.

sections.title: Address Assignment Methods and Binding Anchors
sections.content:
SAVI adapts to the link in two ways. Because it traces address assignment, it comes in variants for DHCP, Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) with or without SEND, IKEv2, and combinations. Separate variants exist so the common case, a link with a single assignment method, stays simple.

The supported binding anchors include:

  • the IEEE EUI-48 or EUI-64 of a host's interface;
  • the port on an Ethernet switch;
  • the security association between a host and a wireless base station;
  • a link-layer address combined with a customer relationship in cable modem networks;
  • an ATM virtual channel, a PPP session identifier or an L2TP session identifier in a DSL network;
  • a tunnel that connects to a single host, such as IP-in-IP, GRE or an MPLS label-switched path.

They differ in strength. EUIs can be spoofed with little effort, and a switch port alone may be insufficient because it may connect to more than one host. The administrator may choose one or more anchors, and a device may have a default such as switch ports when available and MAC addresses otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: Some ways of telling kids apart are strong, like a locked desk. Some are weak, like a name tag anyone can copy.

sections.title: Scaling, Reliability and Mixed Methods
sections.content:
Several SAVI instances must coexist on large links, which would replicate every binding in every instance. To save memory, validation is manually disabled on switch ports that connect to other SAVI switches. The SAVI switches form a protection perimeter: addresses are validated where packets enter it and not again inside. A legacy switch may sit inside the perimeter only if packets cannot enter the perimeter through it. Hosts on subnets attached to non-enforcing ports can still spoof.

Bindings can go missing if configuration packets are lost, a binding is lost in a restart, or the topology changes. To limit the damage, SAVI also creates bindings reactively: when it sees excessive drops from one address, it checks that the address is unique on the link. The SLAAC variant uses Duplicate Address Detection and the DHCP variant uses a DHCP Lease Query to the server.

When several assignment methods hand out addresses from the same prefix, one method's binding may violate another's, for example First-Come, First-Served SAVI against SAVI-DHCP. Collisions are resolved by a prioritization of the methods, which should be configurable. The device also needs correct prefixes, set manually, by snooping Router Advertisements, or by snooping DHCP Prefix Delegation. Manual configuration is recommended unless SAVI is fully deployed, because RA and DHCP-PD messages can be spoofed.
sections.plainLanguage: Guards at every door would need a lot of notebooks. So guards only check at the outer doors, and everyone inside is trusted. If a notebook goes missing, the guard asks the whole room whether a name is taken.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SAVI only mitigates forged addresses. It cannot prove address ownership in a strong sense, and if a binding anchor is not exclusive to each address or is weak, addresses can still be forged. If strong security is required, cryptographic authentication must be used, since it is the only way to provide it.

Placing SAVI close to hosts can make the SAVI devices themselves vulnerable. Deployments should not put SAVI functionality in physically exposed devices, since an attacker could replace the device with one that does not check. Distributing SAVI instances across administrative boundaries, for example both sides of a customer-provider interface, is also not recommended if it requires trusting the other side.
sections.plainLanguage: A teacher who checks names is only helpful if nobody can swap the teacher for a fake one, and a name check is not as strong as a secret password.

viz.caption: THE SAVI MODEL IN THREE STEPS (RFC 7039)

items.title: 1. Identify
items.text: Learn legitimate source addresses by monitoring the host's packets.

items.title: 2. Bind
items.text: Tie each address to a binding anchor that is harder to spoof.

items.title: 3. Enforce
items.text: Drop packets whose source address does not match its anchor.
